en: The Philippine Sea Plate sliding beneath the Eurasian Plate melts rock, feeding Mayon Volcano's frequent eruptions.
Temperature differences between the Asian landmass and the Pacific Ocean drive the seasonal reversal of Philippine monsoon winds.
Tiny coral polyps extract calcium from seawater to build skeletons, slowly forming the massive Tubbataha Reefs.
Heavy rainfall in the Sierra Madre erodes soil, washing sediment downstream to widen the Cagayan River delta.
Magma heats underground water to produce steam, which spins turbines to generate electricity at the MakBan geothermal plant.
Millions of years of ocean isolation allowed the Philippine tarsier in Bohol to evolve its unique, enormous eyes.
Explosive volcanic eruptions collapsed Taal Volcano's magma chamber, creating a caldera that later filled with rainwater to form Taal Lake.
Millions of years of rainwater dissolving marine coral limestone carved the Bohol landscape into the distinct Chocolate Hills.
Strong tidal currents mixing nutrient-rich waters in the Verde Island Passage support its exceptionally high marine biodiversity.
Dense mossy forests on Mount Apo absorb heavy fog and rain, slowly releasing it to feed the Davao River.
Tectonic stress buildup along the Valley Fault System suddenly releases as seismic waves, causing earthquakes in Metro Manila.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone over millennia, carving the massive underground cave system of Puerto Princesa Subterranean River.
